title: Memory Safety: Buffer Overflows, Use-After-Free and Safe Languages
oneLiner: The classes of memory-safety bug (buffer overflow, use-after-free, out-of-bounds read), why C and C++ allow them, the defenses that make them rarer and harder to exploit, and why new systems code is moving to memory-safe languages.
keyTakeaway: Memory-safety bugs are accesses to memory the program was never entitled to, caused by a missing bounds or lifetime check; they are the leading source of critical vulnerabilities in C and C++. Use bounds-aware APIs, compiler warnings, static analysis, sanitizers and fuzzing when you must use C or C++, and prefer a memory-safe language (Java, C#, Go, Python, or Rust for systems code) for new work, since it removes whole classes of these bugs by construction.
explanation:
A large share of the most serious security vulnerabilities come from one root cause: a program reading or writing memory it was never meant to touch. This lesson explains the common classes of memory-safety bug and, crucially, how to avoid them.

It covers why C and C++ permit these bugs, the layered defenses (bounds-aware types, static analysis, stack canaries, NX, ASLR, sanitizers and fuzzing), and why so much new systems software is written in memory-safe languages like Rust. The aim is to recognise the dangerous patterns and pick tools that rule them out, not to exploit anything.
